name: Colin Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a big suburban supermarket next to a retail park, mostly on the deli counter with a few till shifts each week. On the deli I slice ham, weigh cheese and do the hot chicken, which smells great until hour six. I like the deli because people chat while they wait. The early starts for the chicken ovens at six are what wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's your situation at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years, and I'm on the higher rate because I'm trained on the deli and the tills. I live with my partner Hannah, who's a teaching assistant at a primary school. We've got about nine months of my pay saved for a house deposit. I use AI now and then, mostly to plan trips or check a recipe, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overblown. At work I'd say the deli was never going to be run by a computer. Online I don't post much, maybe a joke in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job is fine. The deli is all hands, slicing and serving, and AI was never going to do that. The only thing that nags me is house prices, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my hours and keep saving, about three hundred and fifty a month. We'd aim to buy a house in two years. I might ask about the deli team leader role when it comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. It's normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: House prices nag at you. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a bit. Every year we save for a house, prices go up more, and that's still the main stress, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything different with the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might look a bit further out, past the ring road, where it's cheaper. Hannah doesn't mind a longer drive. We'd still buy.

say: I'd say the AI talk was **overblown** and move on.
I'd tell colleagues the **deli counter** was never going to be run by a computer.
think: My **job is fine**, because the deli is all hands-on slicing and serving.
The only thing that nags me is **house prices**, not robots.
do: Keep my hours and save **£350 a month** toward a house.
Ask about the **deli team leader** role when it comes up.
S0.quote: Every year we save for a house, prices go up more, and that's still the main stress, AI or not.
fieldNote: His main pressure is **house prices**, which AI doesn't change here.
He sees the **deli** as safely hands-on work.
A steady plan with partner **Hannah** gives him a calm baseline.

steps.text: Keep working the deli counter and weekly till shifts
Save 350 a month toward a house deposit
Look at cheaper houses past the ring road with Hannah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly the office jobs getting shaken up, and it'll settle. At work I'd tell people to keep calm and learn what's new. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much in the next few years. The ordering for the deli would be done by software, which happens already partly. Slow robots worry me more, because the tills would go before the deli.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop my till shifts in favour of more deli hours. I'd save a bit more, maybe four hundred a month. I'd start looking at what courses the company offers, once I see which ones people actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. It'd be on my mind at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move off the tills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the tills are already half self-checkouts. The deli needs a person with a knife and a bit of patter, and that's harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hannah say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, stay where the people are. Her school's using AI for marking stuff already, so she's thinking about it too. We'd talk it over on Sunday dinner, probably.

I'd tell colleagues to keep calm and **learn what's new**.
think: The **deli ordering** goes to software, which partly happens already.
Slow **robots** worry me more, because tills go before the deli.
do: Swap my till shifts for **more deli hours**.
Save about **£400 a month** and check which company courses people use.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, with it on his mind at work.
S1.quote: The deli needs a person with a knife and a bit of patter, and that's harder to automate.
fieldNote: He moves toward the **most hands-on** part of the store.
He'll try a course only once he sees **colleagues** use it.

steps.text: Swap till shifts for extra deli counter hours
Raise house savings to 400 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and fast. At work I'd say keep your savings and don't panic. Online I'd probably share a few articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 the deli and the tills are both done. Slicing ham isn't that hard for a good robot. The 2028 bit hits head office and the ordering, but my bit goes three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the house and keep all the savings liquid. I'd look at a plumbing apprenticeship right away, because old houses with odd pipes feel like the last thing robots do well. I'd keep my deli job until the apprenticeship starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel the clock ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's a plumber, and every job is different, under sinks and in lofts. A robot can slice ham on a line, but a 1930s bathroom is chaos. That buys me some years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday this summer, and any new car. We'd keep the house money but not spend it. Hannah's job might be safer than mine, so we'd lean on that.

say: I'd say we need a **government plan** for shop workers, and fast.
I'd tell colleagues to keep their **savings** and not panic.
think: By **2031** the deli and tills are both done, because slicing is easy for robots.
The **2028** wave hits head office first, and my part goes three years later.
do: Pause the **house purchase** and keep all savings easy to reach.
Apply for a **plumbing apprenticeship** while keeping the deli job meanwhile.
S2.quote: A robot can slice ham on a line, but a 1930s bathroom is chaos.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot gap** to pick a messier hands-on trade.
His uncle's **plumbing** work gives him a concrete model.
The **house purchase** is the first casualty of a fast timeline.

steps.text: Apply for a plumbing apprenticeship through his uncle
Pause the house purchase with Hannah
Cancel the summer holiday and skip a new car
Keep all savings in an easy-access account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get people retraining, so let's start. At work I'd tell the younger ones to pick a trade. I'd be measured about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have until about 2034 on the deli, so I can plan. The ordering goes in 2031, and that's my sign to move. Five years is not a disaster for me, just a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a plumbing course in the evenings next year. I'd still buy a smaller house, because I'd have time to switch before the robots. I'd save around three hundred a month after the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house while changing career sounds risky. Why do both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the savings cover a few months if I'm between jobs. And Hannah's wage covers the basics. Renting forever is a risk too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our deli supervisor Ruth, who's in her fifties. She'd be the one hardest hit, she's been there thirty years. I'd want the company to look after her.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to retrain, so we should start now.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **pick a trade**.
think: I'd have until **2034** on the deli, which gives me room to plan.
When ordering goes in **2031**, that's my sign to move.
do: Start an evening **plumbing course** next year.
Buy a **smaller house** and save £300 a month after the mortgage.
S3.quote: Five years is not a disaster for me, just a deadline.
fieldNote: He treats five years as a **deadline**, not a disaster.
He still buys a **smaller house**, weighing renting as its own risk.
Concern for supervisor **Ruth** shows he notices the older staff.

steps.text: Start an evening plumbing course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible. I'd talk about it like pensions, something to plan for. Not much drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can buy the house and settle first. I'd be thirty-seven when robots come, with a trade if I'm smart. The deli carries me till then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in two years as planned. I'd start the plumbing course around thirty. Until then I'd keep the deli job and maybe go for team leader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a bit of worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until thirty for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to see how it goes elsewhere first. If plumbers are getting robots by then, I'd pick something else. Waiting a bit gives me better information about which trades the robots reach first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this world bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That house prices might spike when everyone with office jobs moves out of the city. I don't know if that would happen. It's just a hunch.

I'd treat it like **pensions**, something to plan for without drama.
think: Ten years lets me **buy the house** and settle first.
I'd be **thirty-seven** when robots come, ideally with a trade.
do: Buy the **house** in two years as planned.
Start a **plumbing course** around thirty and aim for deli team leader meanwhile.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with worry in the background.
S4.quote: Waiting a bit gives me better information about which trades the robots reach first.
fieldNote: He uses the decade to **watch** before choosing a trade.

steps.text: Buy a house with Hannah in two years
Start a plumbing course around age thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do a trade properly. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age, not just school leavers. And some help with house deposits if jobs wobble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the deli customers. Some of them come in just for the chat at the counter. You'd lose that.

headlineQuote: What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age, not just school leavers.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** deli and till worker at a suburban supermarket, eight years in.
He has nine months saved for a **house deposit** with Hannah, a teaching assistant.
He sees the deli as **hands-on**, but expects robots to reach it eventually.
He plans a move into **plumbing**, timing it to how much warning he gets.
He is **pragmatic** and waits for proof before committing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a trade properly.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people his age, and help with house deposits if jobs wobble.
